overview: This file consists of four consecutive U.S. Department of State “List of Papers” index pages for decimal file 894.711, summarizing entries 65–87 on Japanese postal laws, censorship, and interference with mail during 1940–1941. The entries document the refusal, opening, detention, removal, and apparent tampering of American diplomatic, consular, missionary, banking, and private mail across Japan, Japanese-occupied China, Manchuria, French Indochina, and Taiwan; they also record diplomatic representations to Japanese authorities, the October 1941 establishment of comprehensive foreign-mail censorship, and exemptions for consular communications in Taiwan. Several entries are cross-references to records filed elsewhere, including a conspicuous group concerning Japan’s petroleum supply and procurement rather than postal censorship.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers for file 894.711, entries 65–87
subfiles.about: A four-page index summarizes and cross-references 1940–1941 records concerning Japanese censorship, detention, opening, and tampering with American mail.
subfiles.summary: Entries 65–75 cover the refusal of commemorative-stamp mail, opening and tampering with official American correspondence, incidents at Nagasaki and Qingdao, and several petroleum-related records filed under other decimal numbers. Entries 76–80 describe difficulties transmitting registered mail through Dalian and Manchuria, the detention of Chase National Bank correspondence, censorship of a missionary letter from Haikou, and discussions with Shiroji Yuki about consular mail. Entry 81 records an October 1941 imperial ordinance authorizing comprehensive censorship and inspection of foreign mail, while the remaining entries concern incidents at Beijing, Guangzhou, Qingdao, Saigon, Hai Phong, Tainan, and Taipei. The final entry supplies references to Taiwan ordinances exempting consular communications from the Temporary Postal Ordinance.

interest: The index is particularly useful for reconstructing a dispersed documentary trail: many incidents were removed from this subject file and cross-referenced to diplomatic-post, China, Manchuria, petroleum, or political-report files. Taken together, the entries show a progression from localized interference and officially disputed tampering in 1940 to a formal, comprehensive foreign-mail censorship regime in October 1941. They also reveal the geographic reach of Japanese controls and the varied American interests affected—embassies, consulates, missionaries, banks, private citizens, and shipping—while the misplaced petroleum entries illuminate the practical inconsistencies of State Department filing.
